text: Anna Stepanovna Politkovskaya (née Mazepa; 30 August 1958 – 7 October 2006) was a Russian investigative journalist known for her reporting on political and social events in Russia, particularly the Second Chechen War (1999–2005). Born in New York City in 1958, she was the daughter of Ukrainian Soviet diplomats Stepan Fedorovich Mazepa (1927–2006) from Kostobobriv and Raisa Aleksandrovna (née Novikova; 1929–2021) from Kerch in Crimea. Her father, ethnically Ukrainian, attended a Ukrainian-language school in Chernihiv before the 1941 Nazi invasion and met her mother at a Russian-language night school in Kerch after the war. By 1952, her father was studying in Moscow, where he married her mother, and later became a founding member of the Special Committee against Apartheid in 1962, serving as its secretary until 1974. Her parents bought an apartment in central Moscow in 1962, where she mostly grew up, attending a music school and training in figure skating, and frequently visiting the Krupskaya Library. She graduated from Moscow State University's school of journalism in 1980 with a thesis on the poetry of Marina Tsvetaeva, under the supervision of Yasen Zasurskii, a close friend of the Mazepas. She married fellow student Alexander Politkovsky in 1978, and by 1981 they had two children, Ilya and Vera. Her initial journalistic work began with a brief internship in the mailroom at Izvestia in 1982, and she later worked as a reporter and editor for the Aeroflot emergencies and accidents section at Vozdushnyi transport, gaining access to travel across Russia. She also worked with the creative union Eskart and the St Petersburg publishing house Paritet. After her husband's declining influence following the 1993 Russian constitutional crisis, her career took off; from 1994 to 1999, she served as assistant chief editor of Obshchaya Gazeta, and from June 1999 to 2006, she wrote columns for the investigative newspaper Novaya Gazeta. She published several award-winning books about Chechnya, life in Russia, and Russia under Vladimir Putin, including Putin's Russia (2004). Her reporting from Chechnya established her national and international reputation, and she frequently visited hospitals and refugee camps to interview victims of the conflict. She documented alleged abuses by Russian military forces, Chechen rebels, and the Russian-backed administration led by Akhmad and Ramzan Kadyrov, including the brutalization of civilians and the systematic torture, abduction, and murder of individuals. In 1999, she helped evacuate elderly residents from a bombed ethnically-mixed home in Grozny. In 2001, she was detained in Khattuni, Chechnya, where she was interrogated, beaten, and subjected to a mock execution using a BM-21 Grad rocket launcher, after which she was poisoned with tea. In September 2004, while attempting to fly to Beslan to mediate during the school hostage crisis, she fell violently ill and lost consciousness after drinking tea provided by an Aeroflot flight attendant, leading to her being taken off the flight and requiring medical treatment in Moscow. She was a U.S. citizen with a U.S. passport but never relinquished her Russian citizenship. She received numerous international awards for her work and used these platforms to urge Western governments to be more vigilant about Putin's policies after the September 11 attacks. In her book Putin's Russia, she accused the FSB of suppressing civil liberties to establish a Soviet-style dictatorship, admitting that society's apathy had enabled the rise of authoritarianism and warning that without information, Russia was hurtling back into a Soviet abyss. She concluded her essay "Am I Afraid?" with the statement that "If anybody thinks they can take comfort from the 'optimistic' forecast, let them do so. It is certainly the easier way, but it is the death sentence for our grandchildren." In May 2007, Random House posthumously published A Russian Diary, containing extracts from her notebook and writings from December 2003 to August 2005, covering the decline of Russian parliamentary democracy, the Beslan crisis, and the "winter and summer of discontent." The book was edited without her input due to her murder on 7 October 2006, the 54th birthday of Vladimir Putin. She was murdered in the elevator of her apartment block in Moscow on that day, an assassination that drew international attention. In 2014, five men were sentenced to prison for the murder, but it remains unclear who ordered or paid for the contract killing. Politkovskaya received death threats, including threats of rape and a mock execution, and claimed that Kremlin officials only spoke to her in secret, outside public view. She also stated that she was targeted for her work, and that people sometimes paid with their lives for speaking out. In 2001, she fled to Vienna after receiving threats related to a police officer, Sergey Lapin, whom she had exposed for torture and disappearances; Lapin was later convicted in 2005. A former fellow officer of Lapin was among the suspects in her murder, with the motive possibly being revenge for her role in Lapin's conviction. The European Court of Human Rights found the Russian Federation responsible for the forced disappearance of Khadzhi-Murat Yandiyev in 2006, and Colonel-General Alexander Baranov, mentioned by Politkovskaya as ordering the detention of militants in pits, was filmed giving orders to execute Yandiyev.

Anna Politkovskaya, an investigative journalist for Moscow's liberal newspaper Novaya Gazeta, was assassinated on 7 October 2006, Putin's birthday, in the lift of her apartment block in central Moscow. She had been shot twice in the chest, once in the shoulder, and once in the head at close range. The murder sparked widespread international reaction. Before her burial on 10 October 2006 at Troyekurovskoye Cemetery, over one thousand mourners paid their respects; no high-ranking Russian officials attended. She was buried near her father, who had died shortly before her. In 2001, she fled to Vienna after receiving email threats from a police officer, Corporal Sergey Lapin, whom she had accused of atrocities in Chechnya; Lapin was later convicted in 2005 for torture and disappearance of a Chechen civilian, a case she exposed in her article "Disappearing People." A former fellow officer of Lapin was among the suspects in her murder, with revenge being a suspected motive. In 2004, Politkovskaya had a conversation with Ramzan Kadyrov, then Prime Minister of Chechnya, who reportedly said, "You're an enemy. To be shot," and one of his assistants suggested she should have been shot in Moscow. On the day of her murder, she had planned to publish a lengthy story on torture by Chechen security detachments known as Kadyrovites. She had described Kadyrov as the "Chechen Stalin of our days" in her final interview. In May 2007, a posthumous collection of her articles, With Good Reason, was published by Novaya Gazeta at the Gorbachev Foundation, shortly after Vera's daughter was named Anna in her honor. In 2008, ten men were detained on suspicion of involvement in her murder; four were brought before the Moscow District Military Court. Three were charged with aiding the killer, who was allegedly the brother of two suspects; there was insufficient evidence to charge an FSB colonel, though he was suspected of organizing the murder and stood trial for another offense. The case was held before a jury, a rare occurrence in Russia, and was open to the press and public. On 25 November 2008, Murad Musayev, a lawyer for the defendants, stated that case notes suggested a Russian politician (not named) had ordered her death. On 5 December 2008, Sergei Sokolov, a senior Novaya Gazeta editor, testified that Dzhabrail Makhmudov was an FSB agent and that his uncle, Lom-Ali Gaitukayev, also worked for the FSB and was serving a 12-year sentence for an attempted murder. After the three men were acquitted in February 2009, Politkovskaya’s children, Vera and Ilya, along with their lawyers and Sokolov, criticized the trial. Andrew McIntosh, a Council of Europe official, condemned the lack of progress in the investigation, calling it a "blatant failure" and urging a relaunch of the probe, citing similar cases like the killings of Georgy Gongadze and Paul Klebnikov. On 19 January 2009, Stanislav Markelov, a lawyer who had investigated abuses documented by Politkovskaya, was assassinated in Moscow; journalist Anastasia Baburova died from injuries while trying to intervene. On 15 July 2009, Natalia Estemirova, a board member of Memorial and a key colleague of Politkovskaya in Chechnya, was abducted in Grozny and found dead in Ingushetia. In August 2009, the Supreme Court upheld the prosecution's objection to the acquittals and ordered a new trial. In August 2011, Russian prosecutors claimed to be close to solving the murder after detaining Dmitry Pavliuchenkov, a former policeman, alleged to be the principal organizer. In December 2012, Pavliuchenkov was found guilty and sentenced to 11 years in a high-security penal colony. In May 2014, five men were convicted of her murder, including three previously acquitted defendants; in June 2014, Lom-Ali Gaitukayev and Rustam Makhmudov received life sentences, though it remained unclear who ordered or paid for the killing. In September 2016, Vladimir Markin, an official of the Investigative Committee, included Politkovskaya’s killing in a list of the Most Dramatic Crimes in 21st century Russia and claimed it had been solved. Her colleagues at Novaya Gazeta protested that without identifying the instigator or sponsor, the case was not closed. On 7 October 2016, Novaya Gazeta released a video in which staff members repeatedly stated, "The sponsor of Anna's murder has not been found." Deputy chief editor Sergei Sokolov published a critical summary of the investigation, describing its false turns and shortcomings, and noted that after the 2014 convictions, the investigative team was reduced to one person who retired within a year, replaced by a lower-ranking investigator. He referenced the 2000 killing of Igor Domnikov, which was later solved, as evidence that perpetrators could be identified. The Intercept published a top-secret document from Edward Snowden showing that on 5 December 2005, the Russian Federal Intelligence Services (likely FSB) launched a cyberattack on Politkovskaya’s webmail account using malicious software not available in the public domain; it was unclear if this attack was linked to her death. Politkovskaya was described as brave, bold, and beautiful, and her fearless reporting on state abuses made her a lonely but powerful voice. A biographical film, initially titled Anna and later renamed Words of War, began production in 2022 with Maxine Peake, Jason Isaacs, and Ciaran Hinds, and had a limited release on 2 May 2025. The 2007–2008 academic year at the College of Europe was named in her honor. The international human rights organization RAW in WAR, founded in 2006 by Mariana Katzarova, established the annual Anna Politkovskaya Award to recognize a woman human rights defender in a conflict zone who stands up for victims at great personal risk. The award was first given on the first anniversary of her murder to Natalia Estemirova, who was abducted and killed in 2009. There is also a "Journalism-prize Anna Politkovskaja" awarded annually in Ferrara, Italy, by the magazine L'internationale and the comune of Ferrara.
